c.tagline: Shikoku's gateway city — sanuki udon, a strolling garden, and ferries to the art islands.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered and plentiful; ride-hailing (GO, DiDi) only dispatches licensed metered taxis rather than private cars, and street and rank taxis are easy to find.

emergency.note: 110 reaches the police and 119 reaches fire and ambulance; English support is limited, so the Japan Visitor Hotline (050-3816-2787) offers 24/7 multilingual help.

hood_desc: The waterfront hub around JR Takamatsu Station and Sunport, with the ferry terminal for the art islands, symbol tower, and Tamamo Park next door; best for first-timers who want transport and ferries on the doorstep.

Downtown Takamatsu's shopping and nightlife core, threaded by the long covered Marugamemachi and Hyogomachi arcades and centered on Kawaramachi station; suits travelers who want restaurants, bars, and shopping at hand.
A calmer district around the celebrated Ritsurin Garden, one of Japan's finest strolling gardens, with quiet residential streets and teahouses; good for a slower, greener stay.
The historic core beside Takamatsu Castle (Tamamo Park), a rare seawater-moated castle by the port; a compact, sightseeing-focused pocket steps from the station.
A residential area on the city's eastern edge below the flat-topped Yashima plateau, site of a famous 12th-century battle, temples, and sweeping Inland Sea views; quiet and local.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Japan.

transit.hours: Kotoden trains and city buses run from roughly 5:30 AM to 11:00 PM; there is no night service, so late trips rely on taxis.
transit.note: Takamatsu's local rail is the Kotoden (Takamatsu-Kotohira Electric Railroad), whose three lines — Kotohira, Nagao, and Shido — fan out from the central Kawaramachi and Takamatsu-Chikko hubs, backed by Kotoden city buses, JR Shikoku trains, and Seto Inland Sea ferries from Takamatsu Port to the art islands.
transit.pay: Tap a nationwide IC card or Kotoden's own IruCa card on trains and buses (a city ride is around ¥200, ~US$1.40); cash is also accepted onboard.

bus: Highway buses to Okayama, Kobe, Osaka & Tokyo
ferry: Takamatsu Port (ferries to Naoshima, Teshima, Shodoshima, Megijima, Ogijima & Uno/Okayama)

transit.m: Airport Limousine Bus to JR Takamatsu Station (~40 min, ¥1000)

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in Japan and can cause confusion; excellent service is standard and already included.

food.name: Sanuki udon
food.desc: Kagawa's thick, square-edged wheat noodles with a famous chew, eaten cold with dipping sauce or in a light dashi broth.

places.name: Udon Honjin Yamadaya
places.note: Hand-kneaded noodles served in a rambling century-old farmhouse - the sit-down classic near Yashima.

places.name: Waraya
places.note: Thatched farmhouse with a water wheel; famous kamaage udon in a communal tub.

places.name: Teuchi Udon Masuya
places.note: Tabelog Kagawa top-100 shop that opens at 11 and often sells out by early afternoon.

food.name: Kama-tama and butter udon
food.desc: Hot straight-from-the-pot noodles bound with raw egg and soy - and Takamatsu's cult butter-and-egg version, carbonara by another name.

places.name: Udon Baka Ichidai
places.note: Made the kama-butter udon famous; queues form early and it is the city's most photographed bowl.

places.name: Tsurumaru
places.note: Late-night udon counter in the nightlife district, open past midnight for post-drinks kama-tama.

places.name: Ueharaya Honten
places.note: Long-running local shop known for kamaage pot noodles and short opening hours - go before lunch.

food.name: Honetsukidori
food.desc: Bone-in chicken leg roasted with garlic and black pepper until the skin crackles - order oyadori for chew or hinadori for tenderness.

places.name: Ikkaku
places.note: The name most locals give first for honetsukidori; several branches, all busy, cabbage and torimeshi on the side.

places.name: Yosuke Shoten
places.note: Popular izakaya-style spot pairing bone-in chicken with beer in the covered shopping street.

places.name: Honetsukidori Ranmaru
places.note: Casual chicken specialist handy for a quick dinner near the station and arcades.

food.name: Olive beef and olive hamachi
food.desc: Kagawa raises cattle and yellowtail on spent olive pulp from Shodoshima - sweet marbled beef and clean, firm sashimi.

places.name: Tenkatsu
places.note: Landmark seafood house with fish swimming in a central tank; the place for local hamachi sashimi.

places.name: Kitahama Alley
places.note: Converted warehouse district whose bistros and grills feature olive beef and Seto Inland Sea fish.

places.name: Takamatsu Central Wholesale Market area
places.note: Market-side canteens serve the day's Seto catch at breakfast and lunch prices.

food.name: Anmochi zoni
food.desc: Kagawa's odd and wonderful soup: a sweet red-bean-filled rice cake floating in white miso broth with daikon and carrot.

places.name: Kanaizumi
places.note: Long-established udon restaurant that serves the anmochi zoni outside New Year for visitors.

places.name: Udon Honjin Yamadaya
places.note: Traditional house menu that includes Kagawa specialities alongside the udon.

places.name: Kikugetsu-tei, Ritsurin Garden
places.note: Historic teahouse serving seasonal Sanuki sweets and mochi looking over the garden pond.

food.name: Shoyumame
food.desc: Roasted broad beans steeped in sweet soy - a humble Sanuki side dish that turns up with udon sets and drinks.

places.name: Marugamemachi arcade shops
places.note: Local food shops along the arcade sell shoyumame and wasanbon sugar as edible souvenirs.

places.name: Udon Honjin Yamadaya
places.note: Serves shoyumame as a traditional side with its noodle sets.

food.name: Sanuki sake
food.desc: Kagawa's rice wine, brewed with soft Shikoku water into clean, food-friendly sake poured all over the Takamatsu izakaya belt.

places.name: Kitahama Alley
places.note: Warehouse bars pouring Kagawa sake with harbour views after dark.

places.name: Ikkaku
places.note: The standard pairing of cold sake or beer with bone-in chicken.

places.name: Kinryo no Sato
places.note: Historic Kagawa brewery with a museum and tasting counter beside the Konpira shrine steps.

food.name: Matcha with wasanbon
food.desc: Whisked green tea served with wasanbon, the fine-grained Sanuki sugar pressed into delicate seasonal shapes.

places.name: Kikugetsu-tei, Ritsurin Garden
places.note: Tatami teahouse over the water; matcha and a wasanbon sweet included with a small fee.

places.name: Marugamemachi arcade tea shops
places.note: Tea merchants and cafes in the arcade sell local sencha and wasanbon boxes.

landmarks: Ritsurin Garden
One of Japan's most beautiful landscape gardens, 400 years of sculpted pines, teahouses and ponds arranged against the borrowed backdrop of Mount Shiun.
Yashima
A flat-topped lava plateau above the city, site of the epic 1185 Genpei battle, with sweeping Seto Inland Sea panoramas from its rim.
Yashima-ji Temple
Temple 84 of the Shikoku 88-temple pilgrimage, crowning Yashima plateau with a vermillion main hall and a quirky shrine to badger spirit Tasaburo.
Takamatsu Castle Ruins (Tamamo Park)
One of Japan's rare seaside castles, whose moats fill with saltwater and sea bream, ringed by pine gardens and a reconstructed turret.
Shikoku Mura Open-Air Museum
A hillside village of relocated historic buildings, from vine suspension bridges to kabuki stages, preserving 300 years of Shikoku rural life.
Isamu Noguchi Garden Museum
The preserved studio and stone-walled sculpture garden of the Japanese-American master in Mure, where 150 works sit exactly as he left them.
Kitahama Alley
A cluster of weathered 1920s harbour warehouses reborn as boutiques, galleries and cafés, Takamatsu's coolest corner for a seaside coffee.
Setoshirube (Red Lighthouse)
The world's first all-glass lighthouse, glowing ruby-red at the end of Sunport's breakwater, Takamatsu's beloved evening-stroll destination.
Naoshima Art Island
The contemporary-art mecca of the Seto Inland Sea, an easy ferry hop away, famed for Yayoi Kusama's pumpkins and Tadao Ando's museums.
Kotohira-gu Shrine (Konpira-san)
Shikoku's most famous shrine, reached by 785 stone steps up Mount Zozu, a classic day trip by vintage Kotoden train from Takamatsu.

train.note: Japan is an island nation with no international trains. Takamatsu's link to the main island of Honshu is the Marine Liner across the Great Seto Bridge from Okayama - the only railway between Honshu and Shikoku - running frequently, taking 55 minutes and costing about ¥1,470, with a cross-platform change from the Sanyo Shinkansen at Okayama. Within Shikoku, JR limited expresses run to Tokushima (Uzushio, about an hour, ¥3,070) and to Matsuyama and Kochi. The private Kotoden runs the Kotohira, Nagao and Shido lines from Kawaramachi in the city centre and is the cheap way to Kotohira-gu shrine; both JR and Kotoden take the local IruCa IC card.

bus.note: There are no international buses from Japan. Highway coaches leave from the terminal in front of JR Takamatsu Station: Osaka is about 3 hours 20 minutes for ¥3,900, Kobe 2.5 hours for ¥3,600, Kyoto 3 hours 40 minutes for ¥4,950, and Tokyo an overnight 10.5 hours from around ¥9,100. Willer Express (https://willerexpress.com/en/) sells English-language tickets and JR Shikoku Bus runs the Kansai and Tokyo services. There is also a direct bus from Kansai International Airport, roughly 3.5 hours for ¥5,150, which is often simpler than flying into small Takamatsu Airport.

Naoshima (Japan) - from Takamatsu Port to Miyanoura, 50 min by ferry or 30 min by fast boat
intl.op: Shikoku Kisen — tickets at the Takamatsu Port terminal counter

intl.to: Uno, Okayama (Japan) - about 1 hour, up to 44 round trips daily, around ¥390
intl.op: Utaka-Kokudo Ferry — tickets at the port counter

intl.op: Shodoshima Ferry — tickets at the Takamatsu Port terminal counter

ferry.note: Takamatsu Port (Sunport) is a five-minute walk from JR Takamatsu Station, which makes this one of the easiest ferry hubs in Japan to use. It is the gateway to the Seto Inland Sea art islands - Naoshima, Teshima, Ogijima, Megijima and Shodoshima - and boats fill up during the Setouchi Triennale and on summer weekends. The Jumbo Ferry to Kobe runs four times a day including a night crossing and is a genuinely cheap alternative to the bus. Foot passengers simply buy at the counter, but cars must be booked in advance, and sailings are suspended in strong winds and fog.

half.name: Tokushima
half.blurb: City known for the swirling Naruto whirlpools offshore and its summer Awa Odori dance festival.

half.name: Marugame Castle
half.blurb: Hilltop castle with one of the tallest surviving stone foundations of any Japanese castle.

half.name: Shodoshima
half.blurb: Island reached by ferry, known for olive groves and a narrow gorge road with dramatic rock walls.

half.name: Megijima
half.blurb: Small island reached by ferry, known for man-made caves linked to the Momotaro folk legend.
